 New York Congressman’s Pet Project: Tax Breaks for Adopting Shelter Animals
 Rep. Tim Kennedy (D-NY) is promoting federal legislation that would offer tax relief to people adopting animals from shelters as a way to help relieve overcrowding at the facilities.
 By Justin Sondel
The Buffalo News, N.Y.
(TNS)
 Rep. Tim Kennedy (D-NY) is promoting federal legislation that would offer tax relief to people adopting animals from shelters as a way to help relieve overcrowding at the facilities.
 The bill, which Kennedy said has growing bipartisan support, would allow people who adopt pets from shelters to receive up to a $500 tax refund on adoption fees each year, a maximum of 50% of the costs, on federal tax bills.
 “It puts money back into the pockets of families, it frees up space and resources at shelters and it gives more animals a chance to find another home,” Kennedy said of the proposed legislation.
 Kennedy also highlighted overcrowding and the aging facilities at the City of Buffalo Animal Shelter. He spoke Tuesday outside the shelter on Oak Street, which is set to be replaced by a new facility on Louisiana Street.
 Across the country, more than 6 million animals were surrendered to shelters, and more than 600,000 were euthanized due to a lack of capacity last year, he said.
 A former Buffalo Police Department substation on Louisiana Street will become the new shelter and replace the dated, cramped and out-of-compliance shelter on Oak Street.
 In June, the Buffalo shelter was over capacity and had to house newly arriving animals in emergency crates.
 “When the shelter ran out of kennel space and had to house newly arriving animals in overflow crates, a story that’s been repeated,” Kennedy said. “Across the country, shelters are facing that same crisis.”
 Kennedy was joined by Buffalo Deputy Mayor Benjamin Swanekamp, who said the adoption tax break would lessen the financial burden on families who want to adopt, but are struggling with tight budgets.
 “Every day, we have dozens of animals going through this facility,” Swanekamp said of the current shelter. “We want to make it as easy as possible for Buffalo residents and folks all across this country to adopt a new shelter pet.”
 Buffalo Mayor Sean Ryan promised to address the poor conditions at the shelter during his mayoral campaign last year.
 Last month, he announced plans to build a $30 million facility in the Old First Ward neighborhood, a project that would increase shelter capacity and provide staff and volunteers with a state-of-the-art shelter that will meet state requirements. The current shelter is out of compliance with state regulations.
 The Ryan administration has also committed $500,000 to improvements and repairs at the Oak Street shelter while the new shelter is under construction. That project is expected to be completed in 2028.
 Jennifer Butera, director of the City of Buffalo Animal Shelter, said making adoption more affordable would help her organization rehome animals—which is beneficial to the animals, the people who adopt them and the city, which is charged with caring for unhoused pets.
 “We are trying to make it more affordable for people to experience the benefits of bringing pets home, which carries with it mental health and health benefits for the humans involved as well,” Butera said.
